org.fullName: The Stanford Initiative for Business, Taxation, and Society
org.tagline: Cross-disciplinary tax research to better inform practice, policy, and academia.

mission: The core mission of our group is to conduct cross-disciplinary tax research to better inform practice, policy, and academia. By bringing together insights from the three fields of Economics, Finance, and Accounting, we seek to contribute new insights that consider how taxation impacts companies, countries, and society at large. We also intend to grow and develop the next generation of tax scholars. We bring together PhD students, post-doctoral scholars, pre-doctoral fellows, and visiting scholars from around the world to discuss and conduct research.

research.intro: Our research studies tax policies at the national, international, and state and local levels. Our research addresses timely and policy-relevant questions, often using confidential administrative tax data. Recent national work includes studies of accelerated (bonus) depreciation and domestic manufacturing benefits. International research examines firm tax planning structures, their timing around IPOs, and how they shape multinational investment and location decisions. State and local research studies the impact of high tax rates on individual residence and the role of tax incentives in firm location decisions.

papers.title: The Race Between Tax Enforcement and Tax Planning: Evidence From a Natural Experiment in Chile
papers.abstract: Profit shifting by multinational corporations is thought to reduce tax revenue around the world. While transfer-pricing regulations are meant to curtail profit shifting, there have been rising concerns that a sophisticated tax-advisory industry can limit their effectiveness. Using administrative tax and customs data from Chile in difference-in-differences event-study designs, we find the reform was ineffective in reducing multinationals' transfers to lower-tax countries and did not significantly raise tax payments.

papers.title: When R&D Incentives Lapse: Corporate Innovation and the Tax Code
papers.abstract: When a key tax incentive lapsed, U.S. companies sharply cut spending on research and development. This paper traces how ambiguity in the tax code causes innovation to falter and quantifies the investment response to the change.

papers.title: Mapping the Maze: Corporate Structures and Unpaid Corporate Taxes
papers.abstract: Complex corporate structures are used by some taxpayers to reduce their tax bills. This work maps where enforcement could recover billions in unpaid taxes and studies how structure complexity relates to effective tax rates.

papers.title: Best-Laid Plans: How Multinationals Minimize Taxes
papers.authors: Clare Doyle, Juan Carlos Suárez Serrato
papers.abstract: An examination of intricate tax-planning strategies used by multinational firms, and of the measurement problems in quantifying their prevalence and revenue impact.

papers.title: Accelerated Depreciation and Domestic Manufacturing Investment
papers.abstract: How accelerated (bonus) depreciation and domestic-manufacturing benefits change the level and timing of firm investment, using administrative data on capital expenditure.

papers.title: Taxes and the Geography of Where People Live and Firms Locate
papers.abstract: State and local research on the impact of high tax rates on individual residence decisions and the role of state and local tax incentives in determining where firms choose to locate.
